newsitem.title: UK: Europe grapples with divided, downbeat economy.
newsitem.headline: Europe grapples with divided, downbeat economy.

text.p: European policymakers and politicians have been scanning the horizons for signs of a long-promised and eagerly-awaited turnaround in the continent's economic conditions.

But economists said latest data reveal anything but the kind of widespread, domestically led rebound that many would prefer to see. French consumer numbers on Tuesday gave the clearest evidence yet that growth is being maintained by external factors alone.
"The continent offers a picture of extremes," said George Magnus, chief international economist at UBS in London.

On the one hand he pointed to countries such as Britain, whose vibrant economic growth is fuelled almost entirely by domestic demand. On the other were Germany and France, where the drivers of what recovery there is were exports and foreign demand.
While a number of countries -- such as Ireland and the Netherlands -- found themselves somewhere in between, a lack of consumer demand in most major European economies was a source of concern.
"Clearly the missing link is this ignition of domestic demand, especially consumer demand, in France and Germany," Magnus said.
Figures from France on Tuesday drove the point home. French consumer spending fell 2.9 percent in June after a revised 0.5 percent drop in May.

Economists noted the data were adversely affected by a relatively small number of crucial Saturday shopping days, poor weather and a late start to summer discount sales at department stores. But the size of the fall was well beyond many forecasts of around 0.5 to 1.0 percent.
"It is really the same story across Europe in terms of the difference between consumption and exports," said Sharda Persaud, economist at Paribas in London.

Some countries such as the Netherlands and Ireland are further advanced in the economic cycle and are showing clear signs of strength, but the dominant theme for much of Europe is that domestic currency weakness has helped export sales, and that this was propping up the economies.
Persaud cited official figures for Germany which showed only a 0.1 percentage point contribution from private consumption to a 0.4 percent increase in gross domestic product in the first quarter.

"Consumers are made insecure by high unemployment," said Jan Hatzius, economist at Goldman Sachs in Frankfurt. "At the moment all we've seen is foreign demand which has picked up quite predictably in response to the dollar."
The dollar has surged against most European currencies, the main exceptions being sterling and the Irish pound, and is at its highest levels against the mark since the 1980s.
But while the current tone was downbeat, economists' expectations ranged from the optimistic to the uncertain.
"We do think the recovery is on track," said Hatzius, who said Goldman Sachs is looking for Germany to show 2.2 percent growth this year and 2.8 percent in 1998.

UBS's Magnus said the strength of the German export sector could have a spillover effect, adding he was more concerned about the plight of French industry, especially with corporate tax increases due to rise.
Analysts said that prevailing loose monetary policies should eventually should bear fruit in the form of economic growth, and it was even possible that fiscal policies could be eased next year.
Until then, said UBS's Magnus, "All we can do is cross our fingers and hope that business confidence is sustained."
